ops.html: Apache Wicket
ops.src: # Apache Wicket

ops.html: Component-based Java web framework. master is the 11.x development line; the maintained release lines live on wicket-10.x, wicket-9.x and wicket-8.x. SECURITY.md says which of them still receive fixes.
ops.src:
Component-based Java web framework. `master` is the 11.x development line; the maintained
release lines live on `wicket-10.x`, `wicket-9.x` and `wicket-8.x`. `SECURITY.md` says which of
them still receive fixes.

ops.html: Versions — the Java release, the Servlet level, library and plugin versions — are not repeated here, because they go stale and then mislead. Read them from pom.xml.

ops.html: How a change lands
ops.src: ## How a change lands

ops.html: • Prepare the change and stop. Whether it goes in as a direct push to master or as a pull request is the committer's call, and the push itself is never yours: don't push, don't open a pull request, don't tag unless you were told to do so.
ops.src:
- Prepare the change and stop. Whether it goes in as a direct push to master or as a pull request
  is the committer's call, and the push itself is never yours: don't push, don't open a pull
  request, don't tag unless you were told to do so.

ops.html: • Fixes go on master first and are cherry-picked down the maintenance lines afterwards, as far as the fix still applies. Which lines are in scope is a decision, not an inference — ask.
ops.src:
- Fixes go on `master` first and are cherry-picked down the maintenance lines afterwards, as far
  as the fix still applies. Which lines are in scope is a decision, not an inference — ask.

ops.html: Commits
ops.src: ## Commits

ops.html: • The subject says what the change does, in plain prose. Issues are filed on GitHub now, and the reference belongs in the body (GitHub issue #1576), not the subject. Older issues still live in Jira; a change that resolves one keeps its WICKET-XXXXX key.
ops.src:
- The subject says what the change does, in plain prose. Issues are filed on GitHub now, and the
  reference belongs in the body (`GitHub issue #1576`), not the subject. Older issues still live
  in Jira; a change that resolves one keeps its `WICKET-XXXXX` key.

ops.html: • The body carries the reasoning: what the behaviour was, why it was wrong, what it is now, and what an application that relied on the old behaviour sees after the change. This is where rationale goes — not into a comment.
ops.src:
- The body carries the reasoning: what the behaviour was, why it was wrong, what it is now, and
  what an application that relied on the old behaviour sees after the change. This is where
  rationale goes — not into a comment.

ops.html: Build and test
ops.src: ## Build and test

ops.html: • A full mvn clean verify has to be green before a change is done. Add -Pjs-test for the JavaScript tests; that combination is what CI runs.
ops.src:
- A full `mvn clean verify` has to be green before a change is done. Add `-Pjs-test` for the
  JavaScript tests; that combination is what CI runs.

ops.html: • Getting there is not how to work there. While iterating, build the least that answers the question: -DskipTests, -Pfast (drops the SLOW-tagged tests, javadoc and sources), -pl <module> -am, -o. Pick whatever is quickest for the task and save the full build for the end.
ops.src:
- Getting there is not how to work there. While iterating, build the least that answers the
  question: `-DskipTests`, `-Pfast` (drops the `SLOW`-tagged tests, javadoc and sources),
  `-pl <module> -am`, `-o`. Pick whatever is quickest for the task and save the full build for
  the end.

ops.html:
• Most tests are not in the module they exercise, so a targeted run resolves the module you changed from the local repository rather than from your working tree, and you quietly test the last thing you installed. Install first, then run the test:

    mvn install -DskipTests -Pfast
mvn verify -pl wicket-core-tests -Dtest=ButtonTest

    -am builds the dependency from source instead, but it applies -Dtest to every module it pulls in and fails on the first one with no matching test, so it needs -Dsurefire.​failIfNoSpecifiedTests=​false alongside.
ops.src:
- Most tests are not in the module they exercise, so a targeted run resolves the module you
  changed from the local repository rather than from your working tree, and you quietly test the
  last thing you installed. Install first, then run the test:

  ```bash
  mvn install -DskipTests -Pfast
  mvn verify -pl wicket-core-tests -Dtest=ButtonTest
  ```

  `-am` builds the dependency from source instead, but it applies `-Dtest` to every module it
  pulls in and fails on the first one with no matching test, so it needs
  `-Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false` alongside.

ops.html: • A test class must be named *Test.java. Surefire includes nothing else, so a FooTests or a TestFoo compiles, passes review, and never runs.
ops.src:
- A test class must be named `*Test.java`. Surefire includes nothing else, so a `FooTests` or a
  `TestFoo` compiles, passes review, and never runs.

ops.html: Where code goes
ops.src: ## Where code goes

ops.html: • A component's markup, .properties, .js and .css sit next to its .java in src/main/java — the pom registers the source directory as a resource directory. The same goes for test pages: their markup belongs next to the test in src/test/java. src/test/resources is not registered at all, so anything put there is off the test classpath.
ops.src:
- A component's markup, `.properties`, `.js` and `.css` sit next to its `.java` in
  `src/main/java` — the pom registers the source directory as a resource directory. The same goes
  for test pages: their markup belongs next to the test in `src/test/java`. `src/test/resources`
  is not registered at all, so anything put there is off the test classpath.

ops.html: • Tests live in the module's -tests companion where one exists. wicket-core has none of its own; they are all in wicket-core-tests, and wicket-​core/​src/​test/java — which does exist — holds only test resources and the JavaScript tests. Modules that have not been split, wicket-extensions among them, keep their tests in src/test/java. Follow the module you are in.
ops.src:
- Tests live in the module's `-tests` companion where one exists. `wicket-core` has none of its
  own; they are all in `wicket-core-tests`, and `wicket-core/src/test/java` — which does exist —
  holds only test resources and the JavaScript tests. Modules that have not been split,
  `wicket-extensions` among them, keep their tests in `src/test/java`. Follow the module you
  are in.

ops.html: • WicketTester, WicketTestCase, FormTester and TagTester are src/main code in wicket-tester, shipped so applications can test against them. A fixture applications would want goes there, not into a test module.
ops.src:
- `WicketTester`, `WicketTestCase`, `FormTester` and `TagTester` are `src/main` code in
  `wicket-tester`, shipped so applications can test against them. A fixture applications would
  want goes there, not into a test module.

ops.html: Poms
ops.src: ## Poms

ops.html: • Section, dependency and plugin order is enforced at validate by the pedantic pom enforcer: dependencies sort by scope, then groupId, then artifactId. dependencyConvergence is on as well. A pom edited in the wrong order fails the build before a single class compiles.
ops.src:
- Section, dependency and plugin order is enforced at `validate` by the pedantic pom enforcer:
  dependencies sort by scope, then groupId, then artifactId. `dependencyConvergence` is on as
  well. A pom edited in the wrong order fails the build before a single class compiles.

ops.html: • A module pom carries no <version> for a dependency. Versions are managed in the root pom, each behind a *.version property.
ops.src:
- A module pom carries no `<version>` for a dependency. Versions are managed in the root pom,
  each behind a `*.version` property.

ops.html: API compatibility
ops.src: ## API compatibility

ops.html: • japicmp fails the build on binary-incompatible changes. Its baseline is the first release of the line the branch is on, derived from the project version: on a maintenance branch that release exists and nothing incompatible can land there, while on master it does not exist yet, so no comparison happens and the plugin only warns.
ops.src:
- japicmp fails the build on binary-incompatible changes. Its baseline is the first release of
  the line the branch is on, derived from the project version: on a maintenance branch that
  release exists and nothing incompatible can land there, while on `master` it does not exist
  yet, so no comparison happens and the plugin only warns.

ops.html: • Quiet is not permission. Changing or removing public API on master is allowed but not free: it needs a justification in the commit message, and where the old member can survive next to the new one, deprecate it rather than remove it.
ops.src:
- Quiet is not permission. Changing or removing public API on `master` is allowed but not free:
  it needs a justification in the commit message, and where the old member can survive next to
  the new one, deprecate it rather than remove it.

ops.html: • An API change owes users a migration path. Add an OpenRewrite recipe to wicket-​migration/​src/​main/​resources/​META-​INF/​rewrite/​wicket.yml where the change is mechanical, and draft the migration-guide wording in the commit message or the pull request description — the guide itself lives on the wiki, where only a human can put it.
ops.src:
- An API change owes users a migration path. Add an OpenRewrite recipe to
  `wicket-migration/src/main/resources/META-INF/rewrite/wicket.yml` where the change is
  mechanical, and draft the migration-guide wording in the commit message or the pull request
  description — the guide itself lives on the wiki, where only a human can put it.

ops.html: Javadoc
ops.src: ## Javadoc

ops.html: • Javadoc is user-facing documentation, not a formality. Public API needs it, and a new public member gets an @since naming the release it first appears in.
ops.src:
- Javadoc is user-facing documentation, not a formality. Public API needs it, and a new public
  member gets an `@since` naming the release it first appears in.

ops.html: • Say what a method does to the value it is given, not only what it returns. Anything bearing on escaping, trust or security — a value written into the markup as is, a template that has to be authored by the developer — is documented on the class or the method, because that is where someone deciding whether it is safe will look.
ops.src:
- Say what a method does to the value it is given, not only what it returns. Anything bearing on
  escaping, trust or security — a value written into the markup as is, a template that has to be
  authored by the developer — is documented on the class or the method, because that is where
  someone deciding whether it is safe will look.

ops.html: Comments
ops.src: ## Comments

ops.html: • Only write a comment when it really matters. Most code should have none.
ops.src: - Only write a comment when it really matters. Most code should have none.

ops.html: • Prefer a clearer name or an extracted method over a comment. Needing one to follow the code is the second-best fix.
ops.src:
- Prefer a clearer name or an extracted method over a comment. Needing one to follow the code is
  the second-best fix.

ops.html: • Comment the why, not the what. Never restate what the line below does or rephrase its intent, and don't comment the obvious.
ops.src:
- Comment the *why*, not the *what*. Never restate what the line below does or rephrase its
  intent, and don't comment the obvious.

ops.html: • Keep an inline comment to a single line of intent, not a paragraph. A class-level comment may be a little more verbose, but keep it a general overview — no implementation detail.
ops.src:
- Keep an inline comment to a single line of intent, not a paragraph. A class-level comment may
  be a little more verbose, but keep it a general overview — no implementation detail.

ops.html: • A comment that no longer matches the code is worse than none. Fix or delete it when you touch that code; that one is not a drive-by change.
ops.src:
- A comment that no longer matches the code is worse than none. Fix or delete it when you touch
  that code; that one is not a drive-by change.

ops.html: • Don't dump your reasoning into a comment. Deeper rationale belongs in the commit message.
ops.src: - Don't dump your reasoning into a comment. Deeper rationale belongs in the commit message.

ops.html: • Before finalizing an edit that adds a comment, re-read it against these rules. Delete it if it restates the code, rephrases its intent, or carries rationale that belongs in the commit message. When in doubt, leave it out.
ops.src:
- Before finalizing an edit that adds a comment, re-read it against these rules. Delete it if it
  restates the code, rephrases its intent, or carries rationale that belongs in the commit
  message. When in doubt, leave it out.

ops.html: Language
ops.src: ## Language

ops.html: • Everything you write is English: identifiers, comments, Javadoc, exception and log messages, bundle keys, commit messages, pull request descriptions and branch names.
ops.src:
- Everything you write is English: identifiers, comments, Javadoc, exception and log messages,
  bundle keys, commit messages, pull request descriptions and branch names.

ops.html: • The localized bundles (Application_​xx.utf8.​properties and their like, around a hundred of them) are translations contributed by native speakers. Add your key to the default bundle and leave the rest alone.
ops.src:
- The localized bundles (`Application_xx.utf8.properties` and their like, around a hundred of
  them) are translations contributed by native speakers. Add your key to the default bundle and
  leave the rest alone.

ops.html: Security
ops.src: ## Security

ops.html: • SECURITY.md is the policy, and it is long: the scope, the conditions under which a report is not assessed, and a security model stating what Wicket trusts. Read it before concluding that something is or is not a vulnerability. A finding that asks the framework to distrust something the model treats as trusted is a deployment issue rather than a framework one — and if the model itself looks wrong, say so about the model.
ops.src:
- `SECURITY.md` is the policy, and it is long: the scope, the conditions under which a report is
  not assessed, and a security model stating what Wicket trusts. Read it before concluding that
  something is or is not a vulnerability. A finding that asks the framework to distrust something
  the model treats as trusted is a deployment issue rather than a framework one — and if the
  model itself looks wrong, say so about the model.

ops.html: • A suspected vulnerability does not go into a GitHub issue, a discussion, a pull request, a commit message or a branch name before a fix is released. It goes to security@apache.org.
ops.src:
- A suspected vulnerability does not go into a GitHub issue, a discussion, a pull request, a
  commit message or a branch name before a fix is released. It goes to security@apache.org.

ops.html: • Working notes, draft advisories and CVE records for an embargoed issue stay out of the repository. Exclude them locally rather than relying on remembering not to commit them.
ops.src:
- Working notes, draft advisories and CVE records for an embargoed issue stay out of the
  repository. Exclude them locally rather than relying on remembering not to commit them.
